title: Imaging Strategies of Non-Conductive Biological Silk Samples
content: Silk synthesis in Arthropods has independently evolved many times, including in moths and butterflies, bees, and spiders [1, 2]. Silk composition and structure diverge across arthropods, which may be influenced by the differing silk uses across the groups [1]. Silk microstructure has been primarily characterized in commercially important species like the domestic silk moth or orb-weaving spiders, given the widespread interest in the mechanical qualities of their silks [3-5]. Meanwhile, in other lesser-known arthropods, the microstructure of silk has not been well-characterized. Trichoptera, commonly known as caddisflies, is an insect order in which larvae synthesize silk proteins in modified salivary glands [6]. Caddisfly larvae deploy silk in freshwater environments, using it to construct a large variety of structures, including nets, retreats, and cases, which may have contributed to their ability to diversify and inhabit a variety of freshwater ecosystems [6, 7]. The scanning electron microscope (SEM) is a valuable tool for studying silk and has been previously used in studies of arthropod morphology and silk microstructure [8, 9]. Determining the optimal parameters for the best imaging quality is a crucial initial step in attaining representative SEM images. Our study aims to determine the optimal SEM parameters for high-quality imaging of Trichoptera silk and sclerotized mouthparts. This will enable us to better characterize the silk diversity within Trichoptera. To do this, we compared different imaging approaches using larval silk fiber and head (i.e., location of the silk-spinning apparatus) samples from specimens of the Hydropsychidae family.
